title: Classic Rock
goal: Play riffs, licks and a written solo in the classic rock style over a band, and know why each note fits the chord under it.
assumes: You can play power chords and single notes cleanly, and eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM. Knowing the A minor pentatonic box helps and isn't required: Step 3 goes through it. Most of the Path is in A, so that theory is the only new thing; licks a player repeats for weeks move to other keys and positions.

skills: Eighth notes with a click at 80 BPM

orderRationale: Riffs come first because they are what a rock player plays most, and they put time in the hands before any theory. The minor pentatonic box and its extension come next, with the licks the style is built on, and then the same box at fret 12 in E, ending with the sextuplet run and its turn back up; the major pentatonic follows, because hearing minor against major over the same chord is the theory that separates rock from blues. Repeating licks come after the box, since they are box notes played as loops. Double stops and chord embellishment, on E and then on open A and D, move from one note to two and into the chord, then chord tones over A, G and D (I, flat VII, IV) show why the same box works over those changes. The slow melody needs control more than speed, so it comes late; call and response with a band uses everything before it, and the sixteen-bar etude puts it all in one solo.
gradingLimits: Graded Exercises are written lines. The app checks timing evenness, notes heard and extra notes on every one, and right notes after the take on single notes that are far enough apart and don't ring into each other; elsewhere right notes read 'not checked'. Double stops, the chord embellishments and riffs with open strings ringing are timed and counted, and not pitch-checked, because a single-note tracker can't tell two notes apart. A bent note would read as a wrong one, so bends are timed and never pitch-checked, and their pitch is a self-check. The right-note check has only been tried on computer-made guitar sound with no band in the mix, so direct input or headphones are the honest way to play anything with a band, and with a microphone and speakers it is untested. Choosing your own notes, landing on chord tones and phrasing are not measured today: those Exercises are 'your turn', self-checked and labelled 'not checked yet'. Nothing here grades feel or tone.

steps.title: Riffs in eighths
steps.goal: Play three kinds of rock riff in time with a band: a single-note root line, parallel fourths, and an open-string pedal.
steps.why: Riffs are most of what a rock guitarist plays, and they are where time lives. A riff played a little ahead or behind is what makes a band sound tight or loose. These three shapes, a root line, two-note fourths and a pedal under a moving line, are the building blocks of a thousand rock songs.
howTo: Palm-mute the low notes marked with an m: rest the side of your picking hand on the strings just in front of the bridge, so they thud rather than ring.
Downstrokes on every eighth sound heavier; alternate if the tempo gets away from you. Either way, lock to the drummer's hi-hat.
Fourths are two strings at once with one finger flattened across them, or two fingers side by side on the same fret.
steps.payoff: You can play a riff with the band and it sounds like a record, tight on the hi-hat.

exercises.title: A root line under power chords

Bar 1: A at fret 5 on the low E twice (muted), C at 8, A, D at fret 5 on the A string, A, C, B at 7. Bar 2: A, A, E and D on the A string, then C and B as quarter notes.
First finger on fret 5, third on 7, fourth on 8. The hand doesn't move.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes on single strings: I check right notes, notes heard and the time after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: The same riffs in E
steps.goal: Play the root line, the fourths and the pedal riff in E: the root line at the nut with open strings, the other two on the same frets one string lower.
steps.why: E is the lowest note the guitar has, and a great many rock riffs are in E for that reason: the open low string is the root, and it is free. You learned three kinds of riff in A. Each of them moves to E in its own way. The root line drops five frets and half of its notes turn into open strings. The fourths and the pedal riff keep their frets and move one string lower. Working that out once teaches you how to move any riff you learn.
howTo: The root line: every note five frets lower than in A. Fret 5 becomes the open string, fret 8 becomes fret 3, fret 7 becomes fret 2.
Open strings ring on after you leave them. Rest the side of the picking hand on the low strings near the bridge for the muted notes, and lift it for the others.
The fourths and the pedal riff: the same frets as in A, on the next string down. The A and D strings in place of the D and G, the low E and A in place of the A and D.
steps.payoff: Three riffs in two keys, and the way to move a riff: by frets, or by strings.

steps.title: The box and its extension
steps.goal: Play the licks rock is built on in box 1 of A minor pentatonic, and reach up to the extension at frets 8 and 10.
steps.why: Nearly every classic rock solo starts in this box. The licks here are its common phrases: a descending sixteenth run, a three-note repeat on the top strings, a six-note sequence that runs down the box, and the extension, the two frets above the box on the top strings where so many solos find their high notes.
howTo: Box 1 in A: first finger on fret 5, the notes A, C, D, E, G. The extension is frets 8 and 10 on the B and high E strings: G, A, C and D.
Play everything at the slowest rung until the notes are automatic, then let the tempo come.
Keep the picking small. Speed in these licks comes from a quiet hand.
steps.payoff: You have four licks you can drop into any A minor rock song, and a way up the neck.

steps.title: The box at the twelfth fret: licks in E
steps.goal: Play the descending sixteenth run, the three-note repeat and the extension lick in E minor pentatonic, with box 1 at fret 12 and its extension at frets 15 and 17.
steps.why: These are three of the licks you already know, seven frets higher. Box 1 of A minor pentatonic at fret 5 is box 1 of E minor pentatonic at fret 12, and nothing in the fingering changes: the same fingers on the same strings in the same order. Two things do change. The frets up here are narrow, so the fingers land in less room than they are used to. And the band is in E minor, the key of the root line you play at the nut, so these licks and that riff belong to the same song. A lick you can play in two places is a lick you can use.
howTo: Box 1 in E: first finger on fret 12, and the notes are E, G, A, B and D. Every fret is the one you played in A plus 7: 5 becomes 12, 7 becomes 14, 8 becomes 15.
The extension is frets 15 and 17 on the B and high E strings: D, E, G and A. In A it was frets 8 and 10.
The frets are closer together here. Keep the fingers curled and close to the strings, and start at the slowest rung while the hand learns the smaller spacing.
steps.payoff: Three licks you can play in A and in E, and a box you can find at fret 5 and at fret 12.

exercises.title: The sixteenth run at fret 12

Four-note groups down the top of the box: E, D, B, A, then D, B, A, G, then down a string.

Bar 1: E at 12 on the high E, D at 15 and B at 12 on the B, A at 14 on the G, twice; then D, B, A, G twice. Bar 2: A, G on the G string, E, D on the D string, twice, then B on the A string and E on the D string to finish.
The same fingers as in A: first finger for every note at fret 12, whichever string it is on, third finger on fret 14, fourth on fret 15.

steps.title: Sixes at the twelfth fret
steps.goal: Play the six-note sequence down box 1 of E minor pentatonic at fret 12 in sextuplets, turn it round at the bottom and climb back up, and end a four-bar phrase in E minor with it.
steps.why: The last Step moved three of the four box licks up to E and left one behind: the sixes, the fastest of them. This Step brings it up. The sequence is the one you know, six notes down the box and then six more from one note lower, on the same strings with the same fingers, seven frets higher. Then two things are made of it. Turned round at the low E, the same sequence climbs. And placed after two bars of slow notes, it does the job a fast lick does in a solo: it answers.
howTo: Box 1 in E, first finger on fret 12. The low E, B and high E strings are frets 12 and 15; the A, D and G strings are frets 12 and 14. First finger for every fret 12, third finger for fret 14, fourth finger for fret 15.

A group is six notes in a row down the box, and it ends on the note it started on, an octave lower. The next group starts one note lower than the last one started. Six groups take the line from G at fret 15 on the high E string down to the low E string.
Learn it in eighth-note triplets first, where a group lasts two clicks, then in sextuplets, where a group lasts one. Either way the first note of every group lands on a click.

Where one group ends and the next begins, the same finger often has the same fret two strings away. Do not lift and hop: lay the finger flat across those strings beforehand and roll onto the new one, letting the old string go quiet.
The sextuplet lick and the turn come back on other days in D, first finger at fret 10, and in C, at fret 8: the same shape and fingers, every fret two or four lower.
steps.payoff: The sixes down the box in A and in E, the turn that takes them back up, and a phrase that uses them the way a solo does: slow notes, then the run.

exercises.title: The sixes in triplets
exercises.purpose: The sequence from 'Sixes down the box', moved to E at fret 12 and played with half as many notes to a click: eighth-note triplets, so every note has room at the slow rungs. Six notes down the box from G, six from the E below it, and so on down to E at fret 12 on the low E string.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, three to a click, 60 BPM up to a pass at 100.

Each group of six lasts two clicks. Bar 1: G at fret 15 and E at fret 12 on the high E string, D at fret 15 and B at fret 12 on the B string, A at fret 14 and G at fret 12 on the G string. Then the six that start from E at fret 12 on the high E string and end on E at fret 14 on the D string.

Bar 2: the group that starts on D at fret 15 on the B string, then the one that starts on B at fret 12 on the B string. Bar 3: the group that starts on A at fret 14 on the G string, then the one that starts on G at fret 12 on the G string and ends on G at fret 15 on the low E string. Bar 4: E at fret 12 on the low E string, held for the whole bar.
Pick down, up, down, up without a break, so that every group starts on a downstroke.

exercises.title: The turn back up
exercises.purpose: The bottom of the lick, and what can come after it. Where the lick stopped, on E at fret 12 on the low E string, this line turns round: six notes up the box from that E, then six from one note higher, five groups in all, to a held E at fret 12 on the high E string.
howTo: Sixteenth-note sextuplets, six to a click, 40 BPM up to a pass at 60.

Bar 1 opens with the last group of the lick, from G at fret 12 on the G string down to G at fret 15 on the low E string. Then three groups go up: from E at fret 12 on the low E string to E at fret 14 on the D string, from G at fret 15 on the low E string to G at fret 12 on the G string, and from A at fret 12 on the A string to A at fret 14 on the G string.

Bar 2: from B at fret 14 on the A string up to B at fret 12 on the B string, from D at fret 12 on the D string up to D at fret 15 on the B string, then E at fret 12 on the high E string, held for two beats.
Inside a group, every move to a higher string lands on the first finger at fret 12. Lay it there while the third or fourth finger is still playing the string below.

Between the climbing groups the line drops back two strings. Three times the finger that has just played has to play again there: the first finger at fret 12 twice, and the third finger at fret 14 once, over the bar line.
The climb is new. Stay at the slowest rung until the first finger finds each string without looking, then move up.

steps.title: Major pentatonic, and minor against major
steps.goal: Play A major pentatonic in two places on the neck, and hear the difference between minor and major lines over the same chord.
steps.why: Minor pentatonic is the tough sound of rock; major pentatonic is the sweet, country-tinged sound of Southern rock and a lot of sixties pop. Over a power chord, which has no third, both work, and the choice between them is the choice of mood. Hearing that choice is the theory.
howTo: A major pentatonic is A, B, C#, E, F#. Its box is the minor box moved down three frets: first finger on fret 2, or on fret 14 an octave up.
The two notes that change are C to C# and G to F#. Everything else in the phrase can stay where it was.
Over A major, use major. Over A5 you choose.
steps.payoff: You can play the same phrase in minor and in major over one chord, and hear the mood flip.

exercises.title: A major pentatonic box
exercises.purpose: The major box up and down, so its notes are in the hand: at fret 2, and the same shape at fret 14.
howTo: Straight eighths, two to a click, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
First finger on fret 2 (or 14), fourth finger on 5 (or 17). At fret 2 the A's are on the low E at 5, the G string at 2 and the high E at 5; at 14 they are twelve frets higher.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

notPooled.reason: Frets near the nut are a wider stretch than up at 14, so each position keeps its own clean tempo.

exercises.title: A Southern-rock major lick

Bar 1, down from A at fret 17 on the high E: A, F#, E, C#, B, C#, B, A. Bar 2: F# and A on the D and G strings, F#, E, then A on the G string held for two beats.

steps.title: The next box up
steps.goal: Play box 2 of A minor pentatonic across all six strings, and a line that climbs through box 1 into box 2 and comes home.
steps.why: The extension at frets 8 and 10 was two strings of something bigger. The same five notes carry on up the neck in a second shape, box 2, which starts where box 1 ends. Nothing about the scale changes: A, C, D, E, G. What changes is which notes fall under which fingers, and that is why a lick played in box 2 does not sound like one played in box 1. Solos that go somewhere are made by moving between the two.
howTo: Box 2, first finger at fret 7: low E string 8 and 10, A string 7 and 10, D string 7 and 10, G string 7 and 9, B string 8 and 10, top string 8 and 10.
Every higher note of box 1 is the lower note of box 2 on the same string. Frets 8, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8 belong to both.
The A's in box 2 are on the D string at fret 7 and the B string at fret 10. Find them first: they are home.
steps.payoff: Twice as much neck for the same five notes, and a way from one box to the other.

steps.title: Repeating licks
steps.goal: Play the looping pull-off licks and open-string repeats of classic hard rock, in time, for as long as the band keeps going.
steps.why: A short lick repeated in time builds tension like nothing else: the crowd hears it coming round again and again. Hard rock players of the seventies built whole solo climaxes this way. The lick is easy; keeping it even, and getting out of it cleanly, is the work.
howTo: Pick the first note of each group, pull off for the second, and pick the third. The pull-off is a small flick down off the string, not a lift.
Keep the fretting fingers for the next note already on the string before you pull.
A pulled-off note is quiet by nature. Make it heard, but don't push the picked notes to match.
steps.payoff: You can loop a lick for four bars and land out of it on the beat, the way a solo builds to its peak.

steps.title: Double stops and rock and roll
steps.goal: Play two-note double stops on the top strings in the fifties rock and roll style, mixed with single-note runs.
steps.why: Two notes at once are louder, brighter and more urgent than one: rock and roll guitar is built on them. The shapes are small, a fret or two on the top strings, and the trick is rhythm: the double stop is a drum hit as much as a melody.
howTo: Barre the B and high E strings with your first finger at fret 5 for the E and A double stop. Your third finger reaches fret 7 or 8 on the G string.
Mute the lower strings with the heel of the picking hand, and hit only the two strings you want.
Play the double stops short and punchy, and let the single notes sing.
steps.payoff: Two bars of double stops into a single-note run: the sound of rock and roll lead guitar.

steps.title: Double stops over E, A and B
steps.goal: Play rock and roll double stops in E over the one, four and five chords: a two-bar figure for each chord, then a twelve-bar chorus made of them.
steps.why: The double stops you learned were in A, and most of them sat over one chord. A twelve-bar rock and roll chorus has three: the one, the four and the five, which in E are E, A and B. Each chord has a double stop that belongs to it, and at the twelfth fret the three sit within a few frets of each other. Play the figures in the order of a twelve-bar chorus and you have a whole guitar part that follows the band, not a lick.

Over A: the G and B strings at fret 14, which are A and C#. Over B: the same shape two frets higher, at fret 16, which is B and D#.
Mute the lower strings with the heel of the picking hand and hit only the two strings you want. Keep every double stop short and punchy except the held ones.
steps.payoff: Twelve bars of double stops that follow E, A and B: a rock and roll chorus.

steps.title: Chord embellishment
steps.goal: Decorate an E and an A chord with hammered thirds and fills between the chord tones, the sixties rhythm-guitar style that sits between rhythm and lead.
steps.why: The most melodic rock rhythm guitar never just strums: it hammers onto the chord's third, slides a double stop into the chord, and fills between the beats. It turns a chord into a little tune, and it is a lesson in where the chord tones live.
howTo: Hold the shape of the chord and lift single fingers to decorate it. Your hand stays in the chord.
The hammer-on goes to the third: G to G# over E, C to C# over A. That half step is the sound.
Let notes ring into each other, and keep the time steady underneath.
steps.payoff: An E and an A that sing, with a fill between them, instead of two strummed chords.

steps.title: Chord embellishment in A
steps.goal: Decorate an open A and an open D chord: the hammer-on to the third you used on E, a new move that adds the fourth above the third and takes it away, and a four-bar part made of both.

The first move is the one you know: the open string under the third is hammered up to it. The second is new: the little finger adds the note one fret above the third, the fourth, and lifts off again. The fourth is one fret above the third on the same string: fret 3, played with the little finger while the finger behind it stays down. Let every note ring into the next, and keep the time steady underneath.
steps.payoff: An A and a D that move inside, and a four-bar rhythm part made of nothing else.

steps.title: Chord tones over A, G and D
steps.goal: Play the triads of A, G and D one note at a time, and licks that end on each chord's root, over the I, flat VII, IV progression of classic rock.

steps.payoff: A four-bar line that follows A, G, D and A, and sounds like it knows where the band is.

steps.title: Phrasing a slow melody
steps.goal: Play a slow, long-note melody over a ballad, in the style of the great melodic soloists, with every note placed and held.
steps.why: The most memorable rock solos are melodies you can sing, with few notes, each one held, bent and shaken. Playing slowly is harder than playing fast: every note is exposed, and the gaps are as loud as the notes. This Step is about choosing to play less.

Add vibrato only once the note has sounded steady for a moment, and keep it even: the same width and speed on every note.
A bend is a vocal slide: it should arrive at its pitch and stay there. Your ear judges it; the app doesn't measure bends.

steps.goal: Play the fast runs and repeating licks a rock solo peaks on, in sixteenths at tempo, and come out of them on a long note.
steps.why: A solo needs somewhere to go. After the melody and the conversation comes the part where the notes get fast, and in classic rock that part is nearly always the same few moves: a run up the box, a lick that repeats, a tumble down in pull-offs. They work because they stop, on one long note.

Pick lightly. Fast pentatonic lines choke when the pick digs in; let the amp do the work.
The long note at the end is half the lick. Arrive on it in time and give it vibrato.

steps.title: A second solo: twelve bars in E
steps.goal: Play a twelve-bar written solo in E minor with the band, from the open strings to the seventeenth fret, then play twelve bars of your own.
steps.why: A solo goes somewhere, and this one goes a long way. It opens in box 1 at the twelfth fret, answers itself with the open-string riff at the nut, climbs back through box 1 into box 2, peaks on a repeating lick and stops on one held note. Every part of it is something you have played in another Step, or close to it. What is new is getting from one part to the next in time, while the band keeps going.
howTo: Learn it in halves, then join them. Bars 1 to 6 are over E5 and A5. Bars 7 to 12 start back on E5, pass through B5 and A5, and end on E5.

Three places for the hand: first finger at fret 12 for box 1, the nut for the riff in bars 3 and 4, and box 2 from the middle of bar 7, where the first finger sits at fret 14 on the D and G strings and at fret 15 on the top two.
The two long moves are made on open strings. The riff starts with two open low E's and ends on one: travel while they sound.
steps.payoff: Twelve bars that start in the box at the twelfth fret, go down to the nut and finish at the seventeenth fret, played with a band.

Bar 5 is back at fret 12: two four-note groups of the sixteenth run, then A, B, D. Bar 6: E, D, B, and A on the G string at fret 14, held.
Bar 3 starts with two open notes, so the hand can leave fret 14 and be at the nut in time for the G at fret 3. Go back up during the open E that ends bar 4.

At the nut: third finger on fret 3, second finger on fret 2, as in 'The root line in E'. Mute the open low E's with the side of the picking hand as you did there, all but the last one, which rings for a full beat.

steps.title: A sixteen-bar solo
steps.goal: Play a sixteen-bar written solo with the band, from the first note to the last, then play one of your own.
steps.why: Everything in this Path, in one solo: a riff-like opening, a sixteenth-note run, double stops, the three-note repeat, and a low ending on the V chord that sends the band back to the top. Learning a whole solo teaches shape: where it starts, where it builds, where it breathes.
howTo: Learn it in halves, then join them. Bars 1 to 8 are over A5, G5 and D5; bars 9 to 16 climb through F5 and G5 to the peak, and come down over E5.
Keep your hand in box 1 the whole way: first finger on fret 5.
Count the rests in bars 3 and 16. The band fills them.
steps.payoff: A whole solo, played with a band, that you could play at a jam tomorrow.
